A FIELD GUIDE TO YOUR LITTLE TROUBLEMAKER

Greed.

When enough keeps moving.

You love options, opportunities, and a comfortably full reserve. Your inner collector is resourceful, alert, and very good at finding one more thing worth keeping.

The meaningEveryday momentsA useful distinctionReading your scoreA little balanceGood questions

A character to get curious about.

THE SHORT VERSION

What does greed mean?

In our quiz, greed follows the little voice that says one more thing will finally be enough. It might be an upgrade, an opportunity, a possession, or a reserve you never quite feel ready to use. The useful question is what happens after a need has been met: can you enjoy it, or does the finish line immediately move?

The good energy

You plan ahead, spot opportunities, and make resources stretch.

The little tripwire

The next upgrade can distract you from enjoying what you already have.

SUSPICIOUSLY FAMILIAR?

Little moments.
Recognizable habits.

These are illustrations, not extra test questions. One familiar moment does not define you.

The unnecessary bargain

You already have what you need, but a limited-time offer makes passing up the extra value feel like losing something.

The next milestone

You reach the target you set. Instead of pausing to enjoy it, you immediately raise the number that would count as success.

The someday cupboard

You keep a useful item you have not touched in years because giving it away would mean losing a possible future advantage.

ROOM FOR NUANCE

Greed and reasonable security

Saving for a real need, negotiating fair pay, and enjoying nice things are not automatically greed. This quiz explores attachment to getting or keeping more. The amount someone owns does not tell you whether these statements fit their experience.

IF THIS CHARACTER SHOWED UP IN YOUR RESULT

Read the score.
Keep the context.

A higher greed score

A higher greed score means our questions about wanting extra value, moving goals, and holding on to resources fit more closely. Consider whether a specific want has a clear purpose. The score does not measure financial success or generosity as a whole.

A lower greed score

A lower score means this small set of acquisition and attachment scenarios felt less familiar. It says nothing about how much money you have or whether your practical needs are being met.

How the number works

Each tendency has three equally weighted questions, answered from 0 to 4. Balancing statements are reverse-scored. The total out of 12 is converted to a rounded score out of 100. Your seven scores are independent; they do not add up to 100. A tie stays a tie.

A score is not a population percentile, a diagnosis, or a fixed personality type. Read the scoring explanation.

A SMALL EXPERIMENT

A little more generosity.

Choose one low-stakes want and write down what it would actually do for you. Set a stopping point before looking at more options. If you already have something that serves the same purpose, try using it with full attention first.

Three questions to sit with

  • What would enough look like for this particular goal?
  • Am I choosing something useful, or trying to avoid missing out?
  • What do I already own that I would not choose again today?

No perfect answer required. Pick the question that feels useful and leave the rest.

BEFORE YOU MAKE IT YOUR WHOLE PERSONALITY

Good questions.

Is ambition the same as greed?

No. A goal can have a clear purpose and a stopping point. The pattern explored here is wanting or keeping more even when the original purpose has faded.

Does being careful with money mean I am greedy?

No. Budgeting and protecting essential resources are practical choices. This quiz cannot assess your financial circumstances and should not be used to judge them.
